{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Early Glasgow Branches in Scotland, c.1447–1650 ==

This page brings together the evidence for people and families using the '''Glasgow''' surname in Scotland from the later fifteenth century to the mid-seventeenth century.

It continues the research begun on '''[https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Bearers_of_the_%27%27de_Glasgu%27%27_Name_and_the_Emergence_of_the_Glasgow_Surname%2C_c.1175%E2%80%931500 Bearers of the ''de Glasgu'' Name and the Emergence of the Glasgow Surname, c.1175–1500]'''. That page establishes the early locative and surname evidence. This page deals with the later transition into documented burgh families, regional surname clusters and early-modern lines.

<small>On this page, '''branch''' means a documented or proposed surname cluster. It does not necessarily mean that descent from another branch has been proved.</small>

The evidence supports four distinct conclusions:

# [[Space:John Glasgow-1|John de Glasgu]] is securely documented as the same Glasgow burgess before and after 1450, in 1447 and 1455;
# the Glasgow surname remained in documented use from the mid-fifteenth century into the sixteenth century;
# a burgh pedigree becomes demonstrable from [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]] onwards;
# several other Glasgow households and regional clusters were contemporary with that pedigree, but their precise relationships remain partly or wholly unproved.

<span id='late_medieval_continuity'></span>
=== 1. Late-medieval continuity and transitional evidence, 1447–1553 ===

The surviving record does not show the Glasgow surname disappearing between the medieval ''de Glasgu'' bearers and the sixteenth-century burgh family.

Instead, a sequence of Glasgow, Stirling, Border and burgh records demonstrates continued surname use:

A [[Space:John Glasgow-1|John de Glasgu]] was recorded as a burgess and property witness in Glasgow on 21 June 1447 and again on 10 April 1455.<ref name="JohnGlasgow1447">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine: Munimenta Fratrum Predicatorum de Glasgu'' (Glasgow, 1846), acts dated 21 June 1447 and 10 April 1455.</ref> Both acts were recorded by Henry Michaelis as notary, and the printed volume's index groups the two occurrences under ''Johannes de Glasgu''. Shared town, civic role, notarial setting and name make this a high-confidence same-person identification.

This supplies a concrete person-level bridge across the conventional 1450 division:

<blockquote>
'''John de Glasgu, Glasgow burgess and property witness, active 1447–1455.'''
</blockquote>

It does not identify his parents, children or later heirs.

A '''John Glasgw''' later witnessed Stirling acts dated 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80.<ref name="JohnStirling1475">''Charters and Other Documents Relating to the Royal Burgh of Stirling, A.D. 1124–1705'' (Glasgow, 1884), acts dated 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80.</ref>

The two sets of records may represent:

* one man active in Glasgow and Stirling;
* two generations of one family;
* collateral relatives;
* or separate families already using the settled surname.

No repeated associate, office, inherited property, seal, notary or explicit relationship presently identifies the Glasgow and Stirling Johns as one person.

The profile or research page covering “John Glasgow, 1475–1536” should therefore not be treated as the biography of one demonstrated individual. The dates 1475 and 1479/80 are documentary occurrences, not birth dates, and no record presently extends the Stirling witness securely to 1536.

[[Space:Alan Glasgw|Alan Glasgw]] supplies a further fixed-form occurrence in a Border record by 26 February 1495.<ref name="Alan1495">Robert Pitcairn, ed., ''Criminal Trials in Scotland'', vol. I, part I (Edinburgh, 1833), p. 19, Jedburgh justice ayre, 26 February 1495.</ref>

On 28 April 1506, [[Space:John Glasgow|John de Glasgow alias Smith]] and Sir Allan Smith jointly acquired an annual rent from property on Glasgow High Street.<ref name="AliasSmith1506">Glasgow University Archives, Blackhouse Charters, GUA BL/204, formerly GUA 16403, instrument dated 28 April 1506.</ref>

Neither Alan nor John alias Smith is connected by a surviving parentage or succession record to the later burgh family.

<span id='transitional_john'></span>
==== A transitional John Glasgow household, 1527–1553 ====

A separate John Glasgow held an identifiable tenement on the west side of the street running from Glasgow Market Cross towards the South Port. On 2 May 1527, a four-shilling annual rent was payable from his tenement, lying north of John Rankyn's land and south of James Young's land.<ref name="OlderJohn1527">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine: Munimenta Fratrum Predicatorum de Glasgu'' (Glasgow, 1846), act dated 2 May 1527, recording a four-shilling annual rent from the tenement of John Glasgu between the lands of John Rankyn and James Young.</ref>

A property inventory dated 5 January 1548 repeated the same annual rent, street position and neighbouring owners. This is the same holding and establishes continuity of the household for at least twenty years.<ref name="OlderJohn1548">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine'', property inventory dated 5 January 1548, again recording the tenement of John Glasgu with the same four-shilling annual rent and adjoining lands.</ref>

On 21 October 1553, John Ranking transferred the adjoining property. Its northern boundary was then described as the lands of the late John Glasgow, establishing that the older John had died between 5 January 1548 and 21 October 1553.<ref name="OlderJohn1553">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', act dated 21 October 1553, describing the adjoining lands of the late John Glasgow.</ref>

This man cannot be [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]], son of William Glasgow and husband of Jonet Spreull, because that younger John remained alive and transferred property to his own son William in 1565.

The older property holder is therefore a distinct and potentially important transitional household. He could have been William Glasgow's father, brother, uncle or collateral kinsman; he could also have been [[Space:John Glasgow|John de Glasgow alias Smith]] of 1506. None of those identifications is yet proved. No inspected record calls William his son, heir, brother or nearest in blood, and no matching succession record has yet been found.

The correct conclusion is:

<blockquote>
'''The surname record is substantially continuous; the civic setting is continuous; the pedigree is not yet continuous.'''
</blockquote>

<span id='proved_burgh_line'></span>
=== 2. The proved Glasgow burgh line ===

The first presently documented multi-generation pedigree begins with [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]].

==== William Glasgow and Esbell Brade ====

A William Glasgow was included in a royal remission dated 2 July 1526 for the slaughter of James Somervile and other offences.<ref name="William1526">''Registrum Secreti Sigilli Regum Scotorum'', vol. I, no. 3433, remission dated 2 July 1526.</ref>

The date and central-Scotland network are compatible with [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]], but the remission supplies no spouse, parent, property, occupation or explicit residence. It should be treated as a possible earlier occurrence rather than a conclusive identification.

William's first secure appearance in the Glasgow town-clerk material is dated 28 February 1530/31. He witnessed a sasine granted by John Wan, bailie, to John Allason in property on Our Lady's Street.<ref name="William1531">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol no. 1058, 28 February 1530/31.</ref>

The decisive family record followed on 31 December 1534. William Glasgow, with the consent of his wife [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]], resigned a back tenement to:

* [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]], described as their son; and
* [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]], John's wife.

William and Esbell reserved the profits of the property during their lifetimes.<ref name="WilliamJohn1534">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol dated 31 December 1534 at 10 a.m., recording the resignation by William Glasgow and Esbell Brade to their son John Glasgow and his wife Jonet Spreull.</ref>

William was dead by about 1543, when neighbouring property was described by reference to the lands of the late William Glasgow.<ref name="WilliamDeath1543">''Liber Protocollorum M. Cuthberti Simonis'' and the ''Rental Book of the Diocese of Glasgow'', vol. II, p. 87, property entry describing the lands of the late William Glasgow.</ref>

No inspected source identifies William as the son or heir of the Glasgow John, the Stirling John, Alan Glasgw or John alias Smith.

==== John Glasgow and Jonet Spreull ====

The 1534 protocol directly establishes:

* [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] as the son of William Glasgow and Esbell Brade;
* [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]] as John's wife;
* and a transfer of identifiable Glasgow property between the generations.

A protocol dated 24 August 1565 records John Glasgow senior resigning a burgage tenement to:

<blockquote>
'''William Glesgw, his son'''
</blockquote>

John reserved liferent to himself and Jonet Spreull, his spouse.<ref name="JohnWilliam1565">Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol. III, protocol no. 847, p. 73, 24 August 1565.</ref>

This proves [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]] as John's son. Jonet was John's spouse and joint liferenter, but the surviving abstract does not expressly call the younger William her son.

A record dated 8 November 1575 identifies [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]] as the son of the late John Glasgow and names Jonet Spreull as his mother.<ref name="Stephen1575">Glasgow protocol abstract dated 8 November 1575, identifying Stephen Glasgow as son of the late John Glasgow and naming Jonet Spreull as his mother. The full volume, protocol number and printed page remain to be added after direct verification.</ref>

The core pedigree is therefore:

: [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]]
:: → [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]]
::: → [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]]
::: → [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]]

Other children should not be attached to John and Jonet solely from repeated forenames, estimated dates or online trees.

A separate protocol dated 8 January 1570 names a '''John Glasgow younger, son of John Glasgow'''. That father-son pair requires independent identification. It should not automatically be merged with John, husband of Jonet Spreull, or with the Stirling witness of the 1470s.

==== Stephen Glasgow and municipal service ====

[[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]], also recorded as '''Stevin''' or '''Stewin Glasgw''', has the strongest surviving civic dossier in the proved line.

His documented activities include:

* witnessing a sasine near Craigmak on 12 May 1574;
* holding land beside Archibald Steven at the burgh boundary in June 1574;
* selling a fore and back tenement to John Scott, baker and citizen, on 17 June 1575;
* acting in property transactions and family business during the 1580s;
* serving as curator to [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]];
* serving as water bailie of Glasgow;
* and continuing to hold or transact in Glasgow property into 1598/99.

<ref name="Stephen1574">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol dated 12 May 1574; ''Records of the Burgh of Glasgow'', vol. I, burgh-boundary perambulation dated 1 June 1574.</ref><ref name="Stephen1575Sale">Glasgow town-clerk protocol dated 17 June 1575, recording Stephen Glasgow's sale to John Scott, baker and citizen.</ref>

The supplied material currently associates Stephen's water-bailie service with both 1585 and a council election dated 4 October 1589. The office is supported, but the precise appointment year or repeated years of service should be reconciled against the original council entries.

Stephen was not himself town clerk. His connection to the town-clerk network is institutional: the burgh's clerks and notaries repeatedly recorded his property, family relationships, curatorship and public office.

==== William, Margaret Herbesoun and George Glasgow ====

[[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]], directly identified as John's son in 1565, married [[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]].

William was dead by 15 July 1586, when [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]] received sasine as his heir.<ref name="GeorgeHeir1586">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol dated 15 July 1586, recording George Glasgow as heir to the late William Glasgow.</ref>

On 1 September 1586, George acted with the consent of:

* Margaret Herbesoun, his mother and liferenter;
* Sir William Herbesoun;
* and [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]], his curators.

<ref name="GeorgeSale1586">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', protocol dated 1 September 1586.</ref>

Because Stephen and William were both sons of John Glasgow, Stephen was George's paternal uncle or half-uncle.

The supported family structure is:

: [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]]
:: → [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]]
:: → [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]] and [[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]]
::: → [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]]

This curatorship and inheritance evidence is stronger than relationships inferred from shared surname, neighbouring property or estimated ages.

==== Robert the fisher, Ninian and John ====

A burgess admission dated 23 October 1596 describes [[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]] as:

<blockquote>
'''second son to Robert G., fisher, burgess'''
</blockquote>

<ref name="Ninian1596">James R. Anderson, ed., ''Burgesses & Guild Brethren of Glasgow, 1573–1750'' (Scottish Record Society, 1925), p. 24, entry dated 23 October 1596.</ref>

Ninian's testament, made on 10 January 1613, leaves:

<blockquote>
'''to Johne glasgw his brother ane new gowne'''
</blockquote>

<ref name="Ninian1613">National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/9, images 142–145, testament of Niniane Glasgw, fisher and burgess of Glasgow, made 10 January 1613.</ref>

The records establish:

: Robert Glasgow, fisher and burgess
:: → an elder or first son John Glasgow
:: → [[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]], second son

[[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]], independently documented as a fisher and Glasgow citizen in the appropriate period, is a strong candidate for the father. The identification should rest on the combined occupation, civic status, place and chronology rather than the surname alone.

Ninian's records also establish:

* [[Meik-14|Jonet Meik]] as his earlier wife;
* Robert Glasgow as the son of both Ninian and Jonet Meik;
* William Glasgow as another son of Ninian;
* and a later wife whose surname is best read as Hutchesoun.

Ninian's brother John was alive in January 1613.

==== John Glasgow in Hirmanscheillis ====

[[Glasgow-3181|John Glasgow in Hirmanscheillis]] died in November 1576.

His testament names:

* Margaret Hoghame, his widow;
* Katherine Glasgow, his lawful daughter;
* Marjorie Glasgow, his lawful daughter.

Katherine and Marjorie were appointed executors-dative to their father.<ref name="Hirmanscheillis1576">National Records of Scotland, Edinburgh Commissary Court, CC8/8/5, image 276 and the upper portion of image 277, testament dative and inventory of Johne Glasgw in Hirmanscheillis.</ref>

This John cannot be the brother named in Ninian Glasgow's 1613 testament.

Any WikiTree relationship showing the Hirmanscheillis testator as Ninian's brother should therefore be removed unless a source establishes that Ninian had two brothers named John.

==== The Corsinkell family ====

The Cunninghame teind material for 1559–60 lists James Glasgow elder and James Glasgow younger at Corsinkell in Stevenston parish.<ref name="Corsinkell1559">Margaret H. B. Sanderson, “The People of Sixteenth Century Ayrshire”, ''Ayrshire Collections'', vol. XIV, appendix “The Cunninghame Teind Lists of 1559–60”, p. 331.</ref>

On 9 February 1571, Corsinkell was described as occupied by James Glasgow elder and by '''James and John Glasgow, his sons'''.<ref name="Corsinkell1571">National Records of Scotland, Charter Chest of the Earls of Glencairn, GD39/5/59, letters of reversion concerning the 40-shilling land of Corsinkell, 9 February 1571.</ref>

This proves:

: [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow elder]]
:: → [[Glasgow-3921|James Glasgow younger]]
:: → a son John Glasgow

The present candidate for the son John is [[Glasgow-3193|John Glasgow]], but no reviewed record yet connects the Corsinkell son directly with Burrowland, Dalgarven or Kilwinning.

No inspected source identifies James elder as the son of William Glasgow and Esbell Brade. The Ayrshire family should remain separate from the proved Glasgow burgh pedigree unless a parentage, succession or migration record joins them.

==== Archibald Glasgow and Isobell Newlands ====

On 21 May 1551, [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]] and [[Newlands-647|Isobell Newlands]], spouses, acquired a fore and back tenement near the South Port and Bridge of Clyde.

The witnesses included a Robert Glasgow.<ref name="Archibald1551">''Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', act dated 21 May 1551. The precise volume, protocol number and printed page remain to be added.</ref>

The transaction securely establishes the couple and their property holding. It does not prove:

* Archibald's parents;
* that Robert was his brother;
* or the children currently attached to Archibald and Isobell.

Those relationships require independent evidence.

==== Robert Glasgow and Margaret Rolland ====

[[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Rolland-239|Margaret Rolland]] were spouses and Glasgow property holders.

Robert appears in burgh records as a fisher and citizen. On 12 February 1572/73, Robert and Margaret transferred property near the Market Cross and South Port. The tenement bordered property belonging to a John Glasgow.<ref name="RobertRolland1573">''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', act dated 12 February 1572/73. The complete volume, protocol number and printed page remain to be added.</ref>

The shared occupation and later burgess evidence make Robert a strong candidate for the father of Ninian Glasgow. That identification is not yet stated explicitly in a record naming both men.

Likewise, Robert's proximity to other Glasgow households supports association but does not define whether they were brothers, cousins, uncle and nephew or members of separate lines.

<span id='regional_distribution'></span>
=== 4. Regional distribution by c.1650 ===

By the later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, the surname was documented in several Scottish regions.

{| class="wikitable sortable"
! Region
! Documented or proposed cluster
! Evidential caution
|-
| '''Glasgow and Lanarkshire'''
| William–John–Stephen line; the older John property holder of 1527–53; Robert the fisher; Ninian; Archibald; other civic households
| Several explicit relationships, but no complete pedigree joining every household
|-
| '''Ayrshire'''
| Corsinkell and Stevenston; Kilwinning and Dalgarven records
| James elder's sons are proved; relationship to the Glasgow burgh line remains unproved
|-
| '''Lothian and West Lothian'''
| Hirmanscheillis; later Kirknewton, Mid Calder, Edinburgh and Leith profiles
| Some profiles rely on estimated dates or unverified parentage and require individual source audits
|-
| '''Stirling'''
| John Glasgw in 1475 and 1479/80
| Important surname continuity; relationship to later Glasgow families unproved
|-
| '''Borders'''
| Alan Glasgw in 1495; later Cavers, Hawick and Berwickshire profiles
| May contain more than one line; no single descent route should be assumed
|-
| '''Argyll and other outliers'''
| Isolated seventeenth-century profiles
| Presence may be genuine, but connection to the central pedigrees requires proof
|}

The evidence supports regional spread and diversification. It does not show that every later regional household descended from the proved William–John–Stephen line.

Several models remain possible:

# some regional households were descendants of the Glasgow burgh family;
# some descended from other late-medieval surname bearers;
# several early Glasgow families may already have existed;
# and some profile connections may be products of later unsourced trees rather than contemporary evidence.

Migration to Ireland, England, the Americas and the Caribbean should be treated on separate pages. Those movements extend beyond the Scottish branch question and often involve distinct seventeenth-century lines.

<span id='marriage_networks'></span>
=== 5. Marriage, property and civic networks ===

The documented households repeatedly married or transacted with families active in Glasgow and the surrounding Lowland regions. One sequence now gives a concrete network bridge from the late-medieval bearer into the family environment of the first proved sixteenth-century pedigree.

==== The Brade–Spreull network bridge, 1430–1534 ====

The sequence is:

* In 1430, a Glasgow tenement on the west side of High Street was bounded on the south by the land of the '''heirs of Walter Sprewl'''. This is explicit inherited Spreull property before 1450.<ref name="Spreull1430">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine: Munimenta Fratrum Predicatorum de Glasgu'' (Glasgow, 1846), Glasgow property entry of 1430 describing the adjoining land of the heirs of Walter Sprewl.</ref>
* On 10 April 1455, [[Space:John Glasgow-1|John de Glasgu]] and '''Andrew Brady''' appeared in the same witness group.<ref name="JohnBrady1455">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine'', act dated 10 April 1455, witness list including Andrew Brady and John de Glasgu.</ref>
* On 27 November 1488, William Sprwl and his wife Joneta Burl sold an annual rent from a Glasgow tenement; '''Robert Brade''' witnessed the transaction.<ref name="BradeSpreull1488">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine'', act dated 27 November 1488, recording William Sprwl and Joneta Burl and witnessed by Robert Brade.</ref>
* On 31 December 1534, [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]] transferred property to their son [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and his wife [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]].<ref name="WilliamJohn1534" />

This is evidence of continuity within a specific Glasgow burgh-property network. The late-medieval Glasgow bearer was operating in the same civic environment in which the Brade or Brady and Spreull names recur, and those two names became the affinal families defining the first proved Glasgow pedigree.

It remains a '''network bridge, not a bloodline'''. No record yet proves that Andrew Brady was related to Robert or Esbell Brade, that Robert Brade was Esbell's father or kinsman, that Walter or William Spreull was an ancestor of Jonet Spreull, or that John de Glasgu was an ancestor of William Glasgow.

==== Later documented marriages and associations ====

Directly evidenced examples include:

* [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]];
* [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]] and [[Herbison-439|Margaret Herbesoun]];
* [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Rolland-239|Margaret Rolland]];
* [[Glasgow-1097|Archibald Glasgow]] and [[Newlands-647|Isobell Newlands]];
* [[Glasgow-3188|Ninian Glasgow]] and [[Meik-14|Jonet Meik]];
* [[Glasgow-1027|Robert Glasgow]] and [[Cunningham-20923|Jonet Cunningham]].

The 1534 marriage evidence places the proved burgh family within a demonstrably older Glasgow Spreull property network. It does not identify Jonet Spreull's exact parents or prove her descent from Walter Sprewl's heirs, William Sprwl, or the Spreulls of Cowden or Ladymuir.

Likewise, the recurring Herbison, Hutcheson, Rolland and Newlands associations are important where they appear in property, curatorship and testamentary records. Their value lies in reconstructing actual civic relationships.

Later appearances of Cunningham, Stewart, Hamilton, Graham, Scot, Fraser and other surnames do not automatically prove marriage into the senior noble or chiefly houses carrying those names. Each connection should be supported by documented parents, estates, marriage contracts, sasines, testaments or equivalent contemporary evidence.

The sixteenth-century evidence is best understood as an overlapping network of:

* burgesses and citizens;
* fishers and maritime workers;
* property holders;
* notaries, clerks and civic officers;
* chaplains and minor ecclesiastical figures;
* and tenant households in the surrounding counties.

Kinship between several Glasgow households is probable. The exact degree cannot be supplied from surname recurrence or a small urban population alone.

<span id='export_limits'></span>
=== 6. What the One Tree export can and cannot establish ===

The One Tree export is useful for:

* locating existing WikiTree profiles;
* displaying current parent, spouse and child attachments;
* identifying geographical concentrations;
* finding profiles requiring review;
* and generating research hypotheses.

It is not itself a genealogical source.

The export does '''not''' prove that:

* [[Glasgow-1095|John Glasgow]] was the common ancestor of the later Scottish lines;
* William, Robert and Archibald were all his sons;
* each displayed parent-child relationship is supported by a contemporary record;
* people with estimated locations were born in those places;
* every Y-DNA-labelled profile belongs to one documented medieval paternal line;
* or a group of connected WikiTree profiles represents one historically proved branch.

A Y-DNA indicator on a WikiTree profile may show that DNA information has been associated with that profile or a descendant. It does not by itself demonstrate descent from the earliest displayed ancestor.

A lineage back to John Glasgow c.1475 and a single paternal root remain possible hypotheses, but the export cannot confirm either conclusion without a documented relationship chain.

The export should be treated as a map of the current tree, not as evidence that the tree is correct.

| Secure father-son and sibling evidence; profile identification still being tested

The best current model is:

: [[Space:John Glasgow-1|John de Glasgu]], the same Glasgow burgess in 1447 and 1455
:: → later fixed-surname bearers in Stirling and the Borders
:: → [[Space:John Glasgow|John de Glasgow alias Smith]] in 1506
::: → a Brade–Spreull civic and property network extending from 1430 to the 1534 proved family transfer
::: → an older John Glasgow household holding identifiable burgh property in 1527–1548, with the holder dead by 1553
:::: → an unproved genealogical connection
::::: → the documented William–John–Stephen burgh pedigree
::::: → overlapping fisher and property-holding households
::::: → separate or partly connected Ayrshire, Lothian and Border clusters

<span id='research_priorities'></span>
=== 8. Research priorities ===

# '''Trace the older John Glasgow tenement after his death.''' Search the 1548–1553 and immediately later protocols for an heir, successor, widow, liferenter or assignee. Priority formulae include ''heres quondam Johannis Glasgu'', ''filius'', ''relicta'', ''proximior de sanguine'' and ''in defectu heredum''.
# '''Identify the late-medieval predecessor of William Glasgow.''' Test whether the older John of 1527–53, John alias Smith of 1506, the Glasgow John of 1447–55 or another bearer can be joined to William by parentage, inheritance, burgess transfer, property succession or repeated associates.
# '''Transcribe GUA BL/204 in full.''' Record the complete alias syntax, witnesses, source of title, adjoining properties and the nature of the joint acquisition by Sir Allan Smith and John de Glasgow alias Smith.
# '''Build the Brade or Brady and Spreull pedigrees independently.''' Search for heirs, siblings, marriage contracts and property succession connecting Andrew Brady, Robert Brade and Esbell Brade, and connecting Walter or William Spreull with Jonet Spreull.
# '''Verify the 1534 protocol directly.''' Add the complete volume, protocol number, page, exact wording, witness list and previous title for William, Esbell, John and Jonet.
# '''Test the 1526 William identification.''' Compare the remission's associates with William's later property, witness and civic network.
# '''Verify Stephen's 1575 parentage record.''' Add the complete protocol citation and transcription.
# '''Reconcile Stephen's water-bailie chronology.''' Check the council records for 1585 and 4 October 1589 and determine whether he served once or repeatedly.
# '''Confirm the father of Ninian Glasgow.''' Test whether [[Glasgow-1096|Robert Glasgow]] is the Robert described in 1596 as fisher and burgess.
# '''Correct the Hirmanscheillis relationships.''' Remove the impossible identification with Ninian's brother John unless new evidence establishes two brothers of that name.
# '''Identify James elder's son John.''' Search for a direct connection between Corsinkell and the Kilwinning, Burrowland or Dalgarven records.
# '''Audit Archibald Glasgow's family.''' His marriage and property are documented; his parents and proposed children are not.
# '''Audit every regional branch independently.''' Do not infer migration solely from estimated profile locations or existing tree links.
# '''Separate migration research.''' Move Irish, English, American and Caribbean lines to dedicated migration pages.

=== 9. Current conclusion ===

The Scottish Glasgow surname was in continuing documentary use from at least the mid-fifteenth century. John de Glasgu is securely the same Glasgow burgess in records of 1447 and 1455, providing a concrete individual bridge across 1450.

A second, more contextual bridge is visible in the Brade–Spreull civic network: inherited Spreull property in 1430, John de Glasgu and Andrew Brady in the same 1455 witness group, Robert Brade witnessing a William Sprwl transaction in 1488, and the Brade and Spreull affiliations defining the proved 1534 family transfer.

A direct pedigree from the late-medieval bearers to the sixteenth-century burgh family has not yet been established. The older John Glasgow who held identifiable Market Cross–South Port property from 1527 to 1548 and died by 1553 is the strongest current candidate for a missing predecessor or collateral, but no surviving record yet calls William Glasgow his son, heir or kinsman.

The first securely reconstructed multi-generation line is:

: [[Glasgow-1098|William Glasgow]] and [[Brade-232|Esbell Brade]]
:: → [[Glasgow-1093|John Glasgow]] and [[Spreull-4|Jonet Spreull]]
::: → [[Glasgow-1029|Stephen Glasgow]]
::: → [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]]
:::: → [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]]

Alongside that line, the records establish the older John Glasgow property household, other Glasgow families at Corsinkell and Hirmanscheillis, and several households within Glasgow's fishing and burgess community.

The current evidence therefore establishes three different kinds of continuity: the same bearer across 1450, a recurring burgh-property network into 1534, and a separate transitional John Glasgow household immediately before and alongside the proved pedigree. Some of these people were probably related. The evidence does not yet show the degree or route of kinship.

=== Contribute ===

Useful contributions include:

* complete archival citations and transcriptions;
* corrections to unsupported profile relationships;
* independent evidence for parentage and inheritance;
* property and witness-network reconstruction;
* and Y-DNA results tied to documented paternal pedigrees.

Tree connections should be treated as hypotheses until supported by contemporary or near-contemporary records.
